questions.question: What is the single medical priority during Care Under Fire?

options.q: Control of life-threatening bleeding
Airway management
Hypothermia prevention
Splinting of fractures

questions.why: Under fire the only medical priority is stopping life-threatening bleeding; everything else waits for Tactical Field Care.

questions.question: Where does a hasty tourniquet go on a bleeding limb under fire?

options.q: High and tight over the clothing
Two inches above the wound on bare skin
Directly across the wound
Across the nearest joint

questions.why: Under fire the tourniquet goes high and tight over the uniform, because you have no time to find the exact bleeding site.

questions.question: Where does a deliberate tourniquet go once you are in Tactical Field Care?

options.q: 2-3 inches above the wound, directly on the skin
Over the uniform at the top of the limb
Directly across the wound edges
Below the wound, towards the hand or foot

questions.why: In Tactical Field Care the tourniquet is applied to bare skin 2-3 inches above the bleeding site.

questions.question: A properly applied tourniquet leaves the thigh still bleeding. What do you do?

options.q: Apply a second tourniquet side by side with the first
Loosen the first and move it lower
Pack the thigh wound with hemostatic gauze
Raise the leg and wait two minutes

questions.why: A severe thigh bleed often needs a second tourniquet placed side by side with the first.

questions.question: How long do you hold direct pressure after packing a wound with a hemostatic dressing?

options.q: 3 minutes
30 seconds
1 minute
10 minutes

questions.why: A hemostatic dressing needs at least 3 full minutes of firm direct pressure to form a clot.

questions.question: A deep groin wound is bleeding heavily and no tourniquet will seat there. What do you do?

options.q: Pack the wound and hold firm direct pressure
Apply a tourniquet across the hip
Cover the wound with a chest seal
Raise both legs above the heart

questions.why: Groin, armpit and neck wounds take no limb tourniquet, so they are packed with a hemostatic dressing and held under pressure.

questions.question: By when should a tourniquet have stopped the bleeding?

options.q: Within 1 minute of starting
Within 3 minutes of starting
Within 5 minutes of starting
Within 10 minutes of starting

questions.why: The standard is bleeding stopped within 1 minute, with the tourniquet fully secured within 3 minutes.

questions.question: In what order does the blood sweep run?

options.q: Neck, then each arm, then each leg
Each leg, then each arm, then the neck
Chest, then abdomen, then back
Head, then chest, then pelvis

questions.why: The sweep starts at the neck, runs down each arm from the armpit, then down each leg from the groin.

questions.question: Which manoeuvre opens the airway when you suspect a neck or spine injury?

options.q: Jaw-thrust
Head-tilt/chin-lift
Head tilt with the chin turned
Chin-lift with the head rotated

questions.why: The jaw-thrust opens the airway without moving the neck, which is why it is used when a spinal injury is possible.

questions.question: What does snoring from an unconscious casualty tell you?

options.q: The airway is partly obstructed
The casualty is breathing normally
The casualty is in shock
The chest is sealed

questions.why: Snoring or gurgling means air is passing a partial obstruction, so the airway needs opening.

questions.question: An unconscious casualty is breathing and has no suspected spinal injury. How do you position him?

options.q: On his side in the recovery position
Flat on his back with the head tilted
Sitting upright against a wall
Face down with the head turned

questions.why: The recovery position keeps the tongue and fluid out of the airway in a casualty who cannot protect it himself.

questions.question: What do you do about debris in a casualty's mouth?

options.q: Remove what you can see
Sweep the mouth with a blind finger
Flush the mouth with water
Leave it and roll the casualty face down

questions.why: Visible objects come out under direct vision; a blind finger sweep pushes debris deeper into the airway.

questions.question: A conscious casualty with facial injuries is struggling to breathe. What position do you allow?

options.q: Sitting up and leaning forward
Flat on the back
On the side with the head down
Face down on the stomach

questions.why: A conscious casualty takes whatever position protects his own airway, which with facial injuries is usually sitting up and forward.

questions.question: Which sign points to a penetrating chest wound?

options.q: A sucking or hissing sound on breathing in
A snoring sound on breathing out
Bright red blood pooling at the groin
Cool, clammy skin on the hands

questions.why: A sucking or hissing sound at the wound means air is moving through the chest wall.

questions.question: You find an open chest wound in Tactical Field Care. What do you do?

options.q: Apply a vented chest seal over the wound
Pack the wound with hemostatic gauze
Apply a tourniquet above the wound
Roll the casualty onto the injured side

questions.why: Every open or sucking chest wound is covered with a vented chest seal, and chest wounds are never packed.

questions.question: Which breathing rate counts as respiratory distress in an adult casualty?

options.q: Over 20 breaths a minute
Over 14 breaths a minute
Exactly 16 breaths a minute
Exactly 12 breaths a minute

questions.why: Breathing faster than 20 a minute, or weaker than 6 a minute, is respiratory distress and goes to medical personnel.

questions.question: Why do you roll the casualty during the respiration check?

options.q: To find entry and exit wounds on the back
To drain blood out of the chest
To warm the casualty's back
To free the arm for a tourniquet

questions.why: A penetrating wound often has an exit in the back, so the torso is checked front and back.

questions.question: Breathing distress worsens after you seal a chest wound. What do you do?

options.q: Burp or remove the chest seal
Apply a second seal over the first
Pack the wound through the seal
Lay the casualty flat and wait

questions.why: Rising distress under a seal suggests a tension pneumothorax, and the first move is to burp or remove the seal.

questions.question: Which set of signs points to shock?

options.q: Rapid breathing, pale clammy skin, confusion
Slow pulse, flushed skin, calm speech
Warm dry skin, strong pulse, clear speech
Slow deep breathing, pink skin, full alertness

questions.why: Shock from blood loss shows as rapid breathing, pale, cool, clammy skin and a casualty losing focus.

questions.question: A casualty with no head injury turns confused and his radial pulse fades. What is this?

options.q: Hemorrhagic shock
Hypothermia
Airway obstruction
A fracture of the pelvis

questions.why: Altered mental status with no brain injury, plus a weak or absent radial pulse, is the field definition of hemorrhagic shock.

questions.question: What do you check on the limb after tightening a tourniquet?

options.q: The pulse beyond the tourniquet
The temperature of the opposite limb
The capillary refill at the ear
The grip strength of the hand

questions.why: A tourniquet that has stopped arterial flow leaves no pulse beyond it; a pulse means it needs tightening.

questions.question: A hasty tourniquet went on over the uniform 20 minutes ago. What do you do now in Tactical Field Care?

options.q: Expose the limb and reapply it to bare skin
Loosen it to restore some circulation
Cover it over and leave it untouched
Remove it and pack the wound instead

questions.why: A tourniquet applied over clothing is replaced with one on bare skin 2-3 inches above the wound, and the time is marked.

questions.question: Where do you record the time a tourniquet went on?

options.q: On the tourniquet strap and the casualty card
On the casualty card only
On the tourniquet strap only
On the evacuation request only

questions.why: The time goes in permanent marker on the tourniquet itself and on the casualty card, so it travels with the casualty.

questions.question: Bleeding is controlled. What is your first hypothermia step for a casualty on cold ground?

options.q: Put insulation between him and the ground
Pour warm fluid over his clothing
Strip his clothing to recheck for wounds
Wait for the evacuation blanket to arrive

questions.why: The ground drains heat fastest, so insulation underneath the casualty comes first.

questions.question: Where does an active warming blanket go?

options.q: On the front of the chest and under the arms
Directly on bare skin at the wound
Wrapped around the head and neck
Under the legs only

questions.why: Active heat goes on the anterior torso and in the armpits, never directly on skin, which would burn the casualty.

questions.question: It is a warm day and your casualty has lost a lot of blood. What do you do about heat loss?

options.q: Insulate and cover him as you would in the cold
Leave him uncovered so he stays cool
Cool him with water to prevent overheating
Cover him only once he starts shivering

questions.why: Hypothermia after trauma is driven by blood loss, not air temperature, so every major bleeder is insulated and covered.

questions.question: What do you do with wet clothing on a casualty?

options.q: Replace it with dry clothing
Leave it in place to hold body heat
Cut it away and leave the skin bare
Wring it out and put it back on

questions.why: Wet clothing pulls heat out of the casualty, so it is swapped for dry clothing and the casualty is covered again.

questions.question: What do you record before giving an opioid or ketamine?

options.q: An AVPU mental status check
The casualty's blood type
The time of the last meal
The air temperature at the scene

questions.why: An AVPU mental status exam is documented first, so any later change can be read against a baseline.

questions.question: A casualty in hemorrhagic shock is in severe pain. Which analgesic fits?

options.q: Ketamine
Oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate
Meloxicam
Midazolam

questions.why: Ketamine is the choice in shock or respiratory distress, where opioids would push the blood pressure and breathing down further.

questions.question: What do you do with the weapon of a casualty who has been given fentanyl or ketamine?

options.q: Take it away from him
Leave it slung on him
Unload it and hand it back
Give it to him for reassurance

questions.why: Casualties are disarmed after fentanyl, ketamine or midazolam, because the drug clouds judgement.

questions.question: Which pair treats mild to moderate pain in a casualty still able to fight?

options.q: Acetaminophen and meloxicam
Fentanyl and ketamine
Morphine and ondansetron
Ibuprofen and naloxone

questions.why: The Combat Wound Medication Pack holds acetaminophen 500 mg twice every 8 hours and meloxicam 15 mg once a day.

questions.question: Which casualties get antibiotics on the battlefield?

options.q: All casualties with open combat wounds
Only casualties with abdominal wounds
Only casualties with burns
Only casualties in shock

questions.why: Antibiotics are recommended for every open combat wound, whatever it looks like.

questions.question: Your casualty is unconscious and cannot swallow. Which antibiotic do you give?

options.q: Ertapenem 1 g by IV, IO or IM route
Moxifloxacin 400 mg by mouth
Moxifloxacin 400 mg crushed under the tongue
Ertapenem 1 g by mouth

questions.why: When the casualty cannot take tablets, the antibiotic is ertapenem 1 g once a day by IV, IO or IM route.

questions.question: Which antibiotic comes in the Combat Wound Medication Pack?

options.q: Moxifloxacin 400 mg
Ertapenem 1 g
Amoxicillin 500 mg
Doxycycline 100 mg

questions.why: The pack the casualty carries holds moxifloxacin 400 mg, taken once a day by mouth.

questions.question: How do you cover a penetrating eye injury?

options.q: A rigid shield taped over the injured eye
A pressure patch taped over the injured eye
A moist dressing laid over both eyes
A bandage bound firmly across both eyes

questions.why: A rigid shield over the injured eye alone protects the globe without pressing on it.

questions.question: Which dressing goes on a partial-thickness burn?

options.q: A dry sterile dressing
A wet sterile dressing
A hemostatic dressing
An occlusive chest seal

questions.why: Burns are covered with dry sterile dressings, because wet dressings strip heat and drive hypothermia.

questions.question: A fragment is lodged in the thigh and the wound is bleeding around it. What do you do?

options.q: Bandage around the object and leave it in place
Pull the object out and pack the track
Push the object deeper to plug the wound
Cut the object off flush with the skin

questions.why: An impaled object is bandaged in place, because pulling it out can open the vessel it is plugging.

questions.question: What do you do with exposed bowel in an abdominal wound?

options.q: Cover it with a moist sterile dressing
Pack it with hemostatic gauze
Force it back inside the abdomen
Leave it open to the air

questions.why: Exposed bowel is covered with a moist sterile dressing or a water-impermeable covering, and never forced back in.

questions.question: What does a splint have to immobilise?

options.q: The joint above and the joint below the fracture
The fracture site alone
The whole limb from shoulder to hand
The nearest joint only

questions.why: A splint only holds the bone still if it takes in the joint above and the joint below the break.

questions.question: The fingers beyond a new splint are cool, blue and numb. What do you do?

options.q: Loosen the wrap and secure it again
Tighten the wrap to control swelling
Take the splint off and move the limb
Raise the arm and leave the wrap alone

questions.why: Cool, blue or numb digits mean the wrap is cutting off circulation, so it is loosened and re-secured.
